The first thing my father repaired after he died was the kitchen clock.

This was inconvenient, because I had already told everyone I did not believe in ghosts. I had said it at the hospital, then at the funeral, and again when my aunt suggested that the robin on my windowsill might be carrying a message.

“It’s carrying a beetle,” I told her.

But on Tuesday morning, the clock began to tick.

It had been broken for eleven years. My father had promised to fix it for ten of them, which was the sort of arithmetic our family understood. For the final year, nobody mentioned it. There were other mechanisms to worry about.

I stood beneath it with my coffee cooling between my hands.

“Very funny,” I said.

The clock continued. It had always been a cheap clock, with a painted lemon on its face. Death had apparently done nothing to improve my father’s taste.

On Wednesday, the cupboard stopped squeaking.

On Thursday, the back door closed without requiring a shove from the hip.

By Friday, I had begun leaving things out.

A toaster with a treacherous lever. A lamp that worked only when its cord lay in a particular, humiliating curve. The little wooden horse I had broken when I was seven and kept in a drawer because throwing it away seemed worse than keeping it broken.

Every morning, something worked again.

There were rules, though I learned them slowly.

He could manage wood, metal, wire, and glue. Fabric defeated him, just as it had in life. I left a torn shirt on the table and found it unchanged beside a repaired stapler I had not realized was broken.

He would not touch anything that still worked, however badly. My laptop remained slow. The refrigerator continued its low, prophetic groaning.

And he never appeared.

I tried staying awake. I sat at the kitchen table with a book open and the lamp burning. Nothing happened until I went upstairs to use the bathroom. When I returned, the wobble had gone from my chair.

“Coward,” I said, but fondly.

Soon the house became intolerably functional.

Drawers slid. Windows opened. The bathroom tap stopped dripping, taking with it a sound I had once hated and now discovered had been keeping me company.

Without the drip, I heard the refrigerator. Without the cupboard squeak, I heard my own breathing. I began to understand how much noise a house could lose before it felt empty.

I missed the noises. I missed him more.

One evening, I put his old wristwatch on the table.

It was not broken. I knew this. I had wound it every Sunday since the funeral. But I wanted him to hold something he had held before. I wanted, absurdly, to give him a familiar job.

In the morning, the watch sat exactly where I had left it.

Beside it was a small screwdriver.

I knew the screwdriver. Its yellow handle had a burn mark from the time he had used it to poke a barbecue coal, insisting afterward that tools should be versatile.

I picked it up.

It was cold.

This disappointed me so sharply that I sat down.

For several days, I left nothing out. The house behaved itself. I went to work, bought groceries, answered messages, and did the ordinary things grief permits once it has stopped demanding every hour.

Then my neighbor knocked.

She carried a radio wrapped in a dish towel.

“I heard you fix things,” she said.

I almost corrected her.

Instead, I asked who had told her.

“Your aunt.”

Naturally.

The radio had belonged to her husband, who was alive but no longer knew what radios were. She wanted to play the cricket commentary in his room. Sometimes, she said, he still turned his head at the sound of applause.

I took it.

That night, I placed the radio on the kitchen table.

“Please,” I said.

In the morning, nothing had changed.

I checked the plug, the switch, the tuning dial. Silence.

For the first time, I was angry.

“You can mend a stapler,” I said to the empty kitchen.

The clock ticked with appalling neutrality.

I went to work. I came home. The radio waited.

Eventually, I fetched the screwdriver.

My father had taught me some things, though at the time I had considered them obstacles between myself and whatever I preferred to be doing. Unplug it first. Keep the screws in a saucer. Never force a part until you understand what is holding it.

Inside the radio, dust lay over everything like felt.

I cleaned it carefully. I found a loose wire near the speaker. I watched three videos, borrowed a soldering iron, and burned my thumb.

At midnight, the radio crackled.

A man was explaining the weather in a place I had never been.

I laughed so loudly that someone knocked on the wall.

The next morning, my father’s screwdriver was gone.

I searched the table, the floor, the drawer where I kept batteries. Nothing.

The clock had stopped, too.

For a moment, I stood very still.

Then I took it down.

Inside was a battery so old that its label had begun to peel. I replaced it with one from the drawer, and the second hand lurched forward.

That afternoon, I returned the radio.

My neighbor turned it on before I had finished explaining about the loose wire. Music filled her hallway, thin and bright.

“What do I owe you?”

“Nothing.”

She frowned.

“Tea, then.”

I stayed an hour.

When I got home, the kitchen was quiet except for the clock. I put the borrowed soldering iron by the door, ready to return, and washed the saucer that had held the screws.

Under it, I found one left over.
